title: How to Spot a Fake Gift Letter
summary: How to spot a fake gift letter: disguised loans, interested-party money, and how to verify the donor's transfer against Fannie Mae and FHA rules.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** A fake gift letter claims that a relative or close friend gave a borrower down-payment money with no repayment expected, when the money was really a loan, came from an interested party, or never moved at all. Cotality estimated that 1 in 106 purchase mortgage applications in the second quarter of 2025 carried indications of fraud. The letter itself is a one-page attestation anyone can type, so the check that matters is the donor's money trail, not the signature.


## What a Fake Gift Letter Actually Is


A gift letter is a signed statement from a donor that names the gift amount, the donor's relationship to the borrower, and the fact that no repayment is expected. Mortgage lenders collect it when a borrower uses someone else's money for a down payment, closing costs, or reserves. The letter is the donor's promise. The bank records that show the money leaving the donor and arriving with the borrower are the evidence.


[Fannie Mae Selling Guide B3-4.3-04, Personal Gifts](https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b3-4.3-04/personal-gifts) , requires a letter signed by the donor that specifies the actual or maximum dollar amount, states that no repayment is expected, and gives the donor's name, address, telephone number, and relationship to the borrower. Acceptable donors are relatives and a defined set of familial or long-standing mentorship relationships. The donor may not be, or be affiliated with, the builder, the developer, the real estate agent, or any other interested party. The lender must then verify that the funds sit in the donor's account or have moved to the borrower or the closing agent.


FHA sets a parallel standard in[HUD Handbook 4000.1, section II.A.4.d.iii(F)](https://archives.hud.gov/offices/adm/hudclips/handbooks/hsgh/4000-1/HB-4000-1-2025-01-10.pdf) . The FHA letter must be signed and dated by both the donor and the borrower. Cash on hand is not an acceptable source of donor funds. Regardless of when the money arrives, the lender must be able to make a reasonable determination that the gift was not provided by an unacceptable source.


Fake gift letters fall into three classes. A disguised loan carries a real donor's real signature over a false promise: the money is expected back. A laundered contribution routes a seller's, agent's, or investor's money through a relative so it reads as a family gift. A fabricated gift has no transfer behind it, supported by an edited donor statement or a made-up wire confirmation. Only the third is a forged document in the usual sense. The first two are true signatures on false statements, which is why the letter alone cannot settle them.


## Why Gift Letters Get Abused


A false gift hides exactly the weakness underwriting is meant to catch: a borrower without the cash to close. Under Fannie Mae's rules, a one-unit principal residence needs no minimum borrower contribution when a gift covers the funds, so the donor's documents can carry the whole cash-to-close.


[Cotality's 2025 fraud report](https://www.cotality.com/resources/reports/2025-annual-fraud-report) estimated that 0.86% of all mortgage applications in the second quarter of 2025 showed indications of fraud, about 1 in 116, and that purchase applications ran higher at 1 in 106. The same report found undisclosed real estate debt showed the largest annual increase of any fraud type, at 12%. A gift that must be repaid is undisclosed debt of another kind.


The losses show up at program scale. A[HUD Office of Inspector General audit](https://www.hudoig.gov/reports-publications/report/nova-financial-investment-corporations-fha-insured-loans-downpayment) found that one lender originated 709 FHA-insured loans with ineligible down payment assistance gifts, putting the insurance fund at risk of potential losses of $48.5 million. In a[New Jersey mortgage fraud complaint](https://www.hudoig.gov/sites/default/files/documents/prnews/Salguero_Jose_Complaint_PR.pdf) , prosecutors said gift letters falsely stated that a relative or friend had provided the down payment when the funds came from an investor running the scheme.


## Tells That Still Work, and the Ones That Don't


The format of the letter tells almost nothing. Lenders hand borrowers a fill-in template, so a clean, generic page is the expected case, and a typo is not evidence of fraud. The tells that survive live in the relationship between the letter and the money.


Read the donor's statement before the letter. A large deposit into the donor's account shortly before the gift, with no explanation, raises the question of where the donor got it. A gift amount out of proportion to the donor's balance history, income, or age earns a second look. A donor whose address, phone, or employer matches the seller, the listing agent, the builder, or the loan officer points to an interested party. The same donor appearing on several unrelated borrowers' files points to a funding source, not a family. A cashier's check with no withdrawal record from the donor's own account leaves the source unproven.


Tell What it still catches What it misses


Required fields on the letter Missing no-repayment language, amount, or relationship Any disguised loan on a complete template


Donor relationship A stated relationship no other record supports A real relative acting as a pass-through


Donor statement history Fresh, unexplained deposits just before the gift Funds the donor borrowed long before the file


Transfer evidence Amount, date, or account mismatch against the letter An edited statement that matches an edited letter


Names and addresses across the file Donors tied to the seller, agent, or builder Ties that only show in public records


Donor reuse across files One donor funding several unrelated buyers A first-time pass-through donor


The tell that fails most often is the one reviewers trust most: a signature. A real donor signs a disguised-loan letter willingly. Any repayment happens after closing, outside anything the lender sees, so the strongest evidence available before funding is whether the money's path makes sense.


## How Detection Actually Works


Detection that holds up treats the gift as a packet: the letter, the donor's statement, the transfer record, the borrower's statement showing the deposit, and the closing figures. Each file gets read on its own, then against the others, through six classes of signal.


Production method asks how each file was made. A donor statement exported from the bank's portal carries a different history from one last saved in a desktop editor or converted from an image, and an edited balance is the usual prop under a fabricated gift. Edited-after-creation, where a genuine bank file was changed after the bank produced it, is a different finding from a page generated from scratch. Timestamp trail asks whether creation and modification times cohere with the statement period and the letter's date. A gift letter signed after the transfer is normal. A donor statement modified the week the letter was signed is not.


Issuer matching asks whether the claimed bank produced a document in this format for this account type, and whether a[wire confirmation](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/how-to-spot-a-fake-wire-confirmation) looks like the sending bank's own record. Consistency sets the gift amount on the letter against the withdrawal on the donor's statement, the deposit on the borrower's[bank statement](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/how-to-spot-a-fake-bank-statement) , and the figure on the Closing Disclosure. Names, account numbers, addresses, and dates should agree across all of them.


Model artifacts ask whether generative tooling left traces that a standard viewer does not display. Recycled patterns ask whether the same donor, the same signature image, the same letter wording, or the same statement file has appeared under another borrower. That last check is the one a single underwriter cannot run from memory, and it is the pattern that exposes investor-funded schemes routed through rotating "relatives."


## What to Do With a Suspect File


A flagged gift is a hold, not a decline. Ask for the evidence the guides already name: the donor's bank statement showing the withdrawal, the borrower's statement showing the deposit, or the electronic transfer record from the donor's account to the borrower or the closing agent. Where the gift arrives at settlement, confirm with the closing agent that the funds came from the donor's account. A line on the Closing Disclosure is not proof of where the money originated.


When the donor's statement shows a recent large deposit, ask the donor to source it. Contact the donor on a number from an independent record, not only the one typed on the letter, and ask plain questions: how they know the borrower, whether they expect the money back, and where the funds came from. A donor who describes a loan has answered the question the letter was meant to settle. Validating[source of funds when documents can't be trusted](https://sphinxhq.com/library/validating-source-of-funds-when-documents-cant-be-trusted) follows the same principle: confirm the money through records the borrower did not produce.


Keep every original file, and do not tell the borrower which signal failed. When the donor statement or wire confirmation is the weak link,[x-ray the file](https://sphinxhq.com/products/doc-fraud) in the Watchdoc playground before calling the donor, so the production history is on record. The first file is free, and no email is required. The broader packet, including income and asset files, belongs in the[loan document fraud](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/loan-document-fraud-detection) review rather than a one-off gift check.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What must a mortgage gift letter include?


Fannie Mae requires a gift letter signed by the donor that states the actual or maximum gift amount, says no repayment is expected, and gives the donor's name, address, telephone number, and relationship to the borrower. FHA requires the same core items in a letter signed and dated by both the donor and the borrower.


### How do lenders verify a gift letter?


Lenders verify the money, not just the letter: the donor's withdrawal matched to the borrower's deposit, or an electronic transfer from the donor's account to the borrower or the closing agent. FHA also requires a reasonable determination that the funds did not come from an unacceptable source.


### Is it fraud if the gift is actually a loan?


Yes. A gift letter states that no repayment is expected, and a lender relies on that statement when it calculates the borrower's debts and contribution. A donor who expects repayment has made a false statement in a mortgage file, even when the signature and the transfer are both genuine.


### Can the seller or real estate agent give a gift?


Under Fannie Mae's rules, the donor may not be, or be affiliated with, the builder, developer, real estate agent, or any other interested party, with a narrow exception for a seller who is also an acceptable family donor and not affiliated with another interested party. FHA treats money from interested parties under separate contribution limits, not as gifts.


### Can gift funds come from cash?


FHA's Handbook 4000.1 states that cash on hand is not an acceptable source of donor gift funds. Both FHA and Fannie Mae ask for documentation that ties the money to the donor's account, which cash cannot provide.
